description: PasswordsCon talks from BSides Las Vegas 2026.

talks.title: PasswordsCon
talks.teaser: Covers OAuth-based authorization phishing, credential leaks in developer tooling, and certificate transparency exposure across four talks.
talks.summary:
This stream opens with a talk on authorization phishing, which goes beyond attacker-in-the-middle proxies that steal sessions after a password and MFA are entered. The speaker covers consent phishing, device code phishing and a consent-based technique that captures OAuth codes. Live demos show a device code kit gaining API access to a Microsoft account even when a passkey is set up. Conditional access tests show that compliant-device requirements and token protection block some variants but not all of them, so defenders need to validate their own policies.

Anthony Hendricks then argues that previously breached credentials, reused and lightly modified passwords, drive many incidents and rising breach lawsuits. He recommends risk-based training, addressing fear of forgetting passwords, and written password policies, and he suggests that adoption of new tools depends on how they are explained to staff. Dwayne McDaniel follows with a look at worm-style package compromises that harvest secrets from developer machines. His checklist includes pinning versions instead of using latest tags, adding a waiting period before updates, disabling install scripts, and moving toward short-lived workload identities.

Kenton Mcdana closes with certificate transparency logs, showing how internal hostnames issued by public certificate authorities can be found without scanning. He walks through the kinds of exposure this reveals and suggests that organizations review what their logs show and ask certificate authorities for private options.

talks.title: PasswordsCon
talks.teaser: Covers credential theft, password cracking, passkeys and identity risks across a full day of talks.
talks.summary:
This full-day stream of the PasswordsCon track opens with a walkthrough of an infostealer-style attack chain, from a malicious file the victim runs through privilege escalation to dumping Windows credentials. The speaker shows how DPAPI-protected browser and vault secrets can be decrypted once an attacker reaches system privileges, and maps each step to MITRE ATT&CK techniques. Later sessions cover password cracking methodology, including attack modes, masks, hash identification and why legacy formats such as LM and NTLMv1 fall quickly while DCC2 is slow.

The middle of the stream focuses on identity. One talk argues that static API keys should give way to cryptographically verifiable workload identities, with SPIFFE and cloud token federation as practical routes. Another looks at passkeys, comparing synced and device-bound variants, and explains how enrollment and account recovery flows can be abused. A third shows that many services accept email addresses as identity, so Gmail dot variants and similar aliases can deliver account notices and recovery messages to the wrong person. A GitLab case study then shows that per-project inbound email addresses can act as credentials that create issues and push code.

The final talks cover the infostealer economy, including malvertising, stolen session cookies that bypass MFA, and operators who infected themselves. The stream closes with honey tokens as decoy credentials and with AI agents treated as non-human identities that prompt injection can steer. The practical takeaways are to treat endpoints as the perimeter, scope and rotate secrets, verify passkey enrollment, and treat email-based tokens as credentials.
